abstract: Background The prevalence of diabetic cognitive impairment (DCI) is significant, some studies have shown that it is related to mitochondrial respiratory chain homeostasis, but the specific mechanism is not clear. 2-hydroxyisobutyric acid (2-HIBA) is a novel short-chain fatty acid with potential applications in the treatment of metabolic diseases because it can regulate mitochondrial disorders. Our aim was to explore a novel mechanism of action for 2-HIBA in the treatment of DCI in mitochondrial respiratory chain homeostasis. Methods Metabolic substances and differentially active metabolic pathways in the serum of diseased mice were identified based on multi-omics analysis. The nanoLC-Obitrap-MS technology was utilized to detect the content of selected small molecules with differential metabolic activity in the hippocampus and mitochondria of mice to evaluate their permeability through the blood-brain barrier (BBB) and outer mitochondrial membrane. A combination of behavioral, proteomic, and molecular biology approaches was used to explore specific regulatory mechanisms and identify potential pharmacological targets. Additionally, using techniques such as protein thermal shift, drug affinity responsive target stability (DARTS), hydrolase stability, and surface plasmon resonance (SPR) experiments, we demonstrated the direct binding effects of small molecule metabolites with protein targets. Results 2-HIBA was found to directly ameliorate cognitive dysfunction in db/db mice by penetrating the blood-brain barrier and reversing the decrease in the protein content of NADH dehydrogenase 3 (MT-ND3) in the hippocampus through direct binding to ND3. This action helps maintain the stability of NAD + /NADH and regulate the mitochondrial respiratory chain balance. Furthermore, a combined medication plant agonist of 2-HIBA can enhance the expression of MT-ND3, thereby improving cognitive dysfunction in mice. Conclusion MT-ND3 is a crucial target for improving diabetic cognitive dysfunction, and 2-HIBA can directly bind to the MT-ND3 protein to alleviate the functional impairment of the mitochondrial respiratory chain in mice to treat DCI.

Barnes maze test
After 6 weeks of drug treatment, the Barnes maze test was performed to detect the spatial learning and memory abilities of the mice. The Barnes maze test was designed to take advantage of the preference of mice for darkness and the avoidance of light. Under certain external stimuli, mice were able to locate the corresponding holes in the dark box within a specified time. The experiment was divided into two training periods and a testing period. After several consecutive days of training, the latency time (the time the mice entered the dark box), the target quadrant ratio (the number of times the mice entered the wrong hole), and the road map were recorded. To ensure that the openings were randomly distributed after each experiment, the location of the maze was different for two consecutive days and the position of the target box was not changed during this process. As the mouse wandered into the cave and its head stuck in the hole, its eyes were lower than the edge of the platform to judge the escape error.

Twenty-four hours after the last day of 2-HIBA treatment, the mice were provided with fresh nesting material and cotton nestlets in their home cages. Photographs of the nests were recorded at the beginning of the light cycle and rated on a scale of 1–5 by two blinded analysts. A score of 1 indicated a completely unconstructed nest, whereas a score of 5 indicated a completed nest that integrated all the available materials.

GraphPad Prism version 9.0.0 was used for all the statistical analyses.

Introduction
Diabetic cognitive impairment (DCI) is a common dementia disease that refers to the abnormal brain function resulting from metabolic disorders and microvascular lesions associated with diabetes mellitus (DM). Typical clinical symptoms include cognition, learning, and memory abnormalities due to high glucose levels in diabetes and loss of spoken language. Mild cognitive impairment is observed in 25 % of patients with diabetic encephalopathy [
1
], and approximately one-third of older adults with diabetes have cognitive impairment [
2
]. The pathogenesis of DCI involves various factors, but its underlying mechanism remains highly complex and unclear. At present, metformin is the most classic drug to treat diabetes, but long-term use will lead to vitamin B12 deficiency, but will increase the incidence of dementia in diabetes patients [
3
,
4
]. Other drugs also have adverse effects, such as kidney and cardiovascular system damage, depression, severe skin allergies, gastrointestinal reactions, vertigo and so on [
5
,
6
]. Accordingly, it is necessary to propose an effective treatment for diabetic cognitive dysfunction. Some studies have shown that the production of DCI may be associated in the mitochondrial respiratory chain [
7
,
8
]. The mitochondrial redox imbalance occurs before the measurable cognitive decline in 8-week-old diabetic mice [
9
]. Therefore, the development of novel pharmacological strategies and therapeutic drugs is imperative.
In recent years, an increasing number of studies have demonstrated the crucial role of mitochondrial damage in the pathogenesis of diabetes and neurodegenerative diseases [
10
]. The regulation of mitochondrial function is dynamically controlled by both nuclear DNA (nDNA) and mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). The latter encodes only 13 proteins, most of which serve as subunits of essential enzymes within the mitochondrial respiratory chain complex, and are vital for maintaining oxidative phosphorylation. Mitochondrial NADH-dehydrogenase 3 (ND3) is a significant protein encoded by the mtDNA chain, and has been identified as a key component of complex I of the mitochondrial respiratory chain [
11
]. It plays a critical role in ensuring the proper assembly of complex I, and ND3 mutations result in severe dysfunction within this respiratory system, leading to hereditary central neurodegenerative diseases associated with mitochondria [
12
]. MT-ND subunits play an important role in constructing mitochondrial respiratory chain homeostasis [
13
]. It has been shown that the expression of the gene encoding MT-ND3 is significantly downregulated during mitochondrial dysfunction, along with the mitochondrial respiratory chain disorder [
14
]. Some scholars have found that the mitochondrial function in the brain of depressed patients is impaired, and that the genes encoding the MT-ND family are altered simultaneously [
15
]. Previous studies have linked ND3 and ND6 from the MT-ND protein family to the onset of type II diabetes [
16
]. Therefore, we propose that selectively targeting mitochondrial ND proteins represents a potential therapeutic strategy for addressing DM-related neuronal cell damage.
In this study, we applied metabolomics to screen for 2-hydroxybutyric acid (2-HIBA), a microbially derived fatty acid metabolite found in the digestive tract, urine, and serum. It is closely associated with metabolism and diseases, particularly metabolic disorders and diabetes [
17
]. There are few studies. Recent studies suggest that 2-HIBA may be involved in lipid and fatty acid metabolism, delay the aging process, and stimulate stress response to extend the lifespan of
Caenorhabditis elegans
[
18
]. And the concentration of 2-HIBA in urine can serve as a biomarker for assessing the metabolic status and diagnosing related diseases [
19
]. However, whether it can be used to treat diabetes and neurodegenerative diseases by regulating mitochondrial respiratory chain homeostasis, as well as its specific biological significance, remains unknown.
Therefore, we performed a detailed analysis of its biological metabolism and potential molecular target mechanisms. We herein report that the MT-ND3 subunit protein in the NADH respiratory chain complex enzyme can serve as a promising drug target for preventing nerve damage caused by hyperglycemic environments. The natural drugs, Gegen Qinlian decoction (GQD), related to mitochondrial homeostasis were screened through network pharmacology, and the functions as agonists of 2-HIBA were explored, eventually increased the content of MT-ND3 and improve cognitive dysfunction in mice. This study may contribute to the development of new targeted drugs for the treatment of diabetes with nerve injuries.

Fig. 1

Among these products, 2-HIBA, a common small-molecule fatty acid metabolite produced by intestinal microorganisms, is produced in vivo and is associated with metabolism and diseases, especially metabolic disorders, diabetes, and mitochondrial dysfunction [
18
,
20
,
21

21

22
,
23

24

Considering the specific nature of MT-ND3 as a mitochondrial DNA-encoded protein, we assessed the feasibility of AAV viral vectors entering the mitochondria to inhibit its expression. Previous studies have demonstrated the successful entry of siRNA into the mitochondria and the subsequent knockdown of mitochondrial encoded proteins [

The mechanism of action of the AAV virus vector is the transport of specific shRNAs to designated tissue sites and their release; shRNAs eventually transform from double-stranded to single-stranded siRNAs to exert inhibitory effects. Therefore, the theoretical feasibility of this method was determined.

Discussion
Developing therapeutic options to treat cognitive impairment in diabetic encephalopathy is critical for extending the lifespan of affected individuals. The formation of hyperglycemia is a basic biochemical abnormality and an important factor in neuronal cell damage during the pathogenesis of diabetes. Here, we describe a small-molecule metabolite, 2-HIBA, derived from intestinal microbes whose structure is similar to that of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA), a short- and medium-chain fatty acid with neuroprotective potential. Studies have shown that SCFAs are the main metabolites released by the intestinal flora that can cross the BBB through monocarboxylic acid transporters and act on the brain [
58
]. SCFAs supplements can promote the production of mouse fibroblast growth factor-21 thereby activating the adenosine 5′-monophosphate (AMP)-activated protein kinase/sirtuin1 (AMPK/Sirt1) signaling pathway and inhibiting the mTOR signaling pathway, increase the growth of hippocampal nerves in the brain, and improve memory function in mice with AD [
59
]. SCFAs is a new target for studying the mechanisms of degenerative diseases, which can inhibit inflammatory responses, regulate circulation metabolism, enhance microglial phagocytosis, and improve amyloid β (Aβ) deposition [
60
]. Studies have shown that in rodent models, age-related changes in spatial memory are accompanied by a decrease in the number of interneurons expressing the GABA-synthesizing enzyme glutamate decarboxylase (GAD) in the medial temporal lobe [
61
], and reduced GABAergic transmission aggravates neurophysiological damage [
62
]. Therefore, we believe that 2-HIBA is a potential therapeutic drug for diabetic neuropathy. To verify this, we intragastrically administered 2-HIBA to 9-week-old db/db mice with cognitive dysfunction and found that 2-HIBA administration reduced the latency of mice in the maze and increased their latency ratio in the target quadrant (
Fig. 2
C), indicating that 2-HIBA greatly improved diabetes-induced cognitive dysfunction. Simultaneously, the diabetic symptoms of db/db mice also improved, as shown by the stable decrease in blood sugar after 6 weeks of administration (
Fig. 2
E) and higher blood sugar recovery ability and insulin sensitivity in glucose tolerance and insulin resistance experiments (
Fig. 2
F). We also successfully reduced the phosphorylation level of Tau protein in the hippocampal tissue of their brains (
Fig. 2
G). 2-HIBA content in the brains of mice increased significantly after administration, indicating that HIBA can directly act on the brain through the BBB (
Fig. 3
), and pathological analysis further showed that intervention with 2-HIBA improved neuronal morphology (
Fig. 2
I), and significantly improved mitochondrial energy metabolism homeostasis.
Proteomic analysis showed significant differences in the mitochondrial transmembrane protein MT-ND3 between each group and the treatment group (
Fig. 4
B). After administration of 2-HIBA and GQD, the levels of mitochondrial transmembrane proteins in mice with diabetic encephalopathy increased. Studies have shown that patients with diabetes or neurodegenerative diseases have large energy metabolism defects [
31
]. NADH reduced coenzyme I is an important coenzyme protein in the energy supply of the respiratory chain, and its damage plays an important role in the occurrence of diseases. ND3 is a protein that plays an important role in homeostasis. As a mitochondrial autoencoded protein, its variation may lead to severe neurodegenerative diseases and metabolic diseases [
32
,
33
]. However, its biological significance and role in the pathogenesis of diabetic encephalopathy have not yet been reported. Therefore, we speculate that MT-ND3 may be a key target of HIBA in the treatment of diabetic encephalopathy. Our study showed that when ND3 was knocked down, 2-HIBA no longer restored energy supply homeostasis and mitochondrial number in nerve cells damaged by high glucose (
Fig. 4
F–H). In vivo studies also showed that ND3 knockdown blocked the effect of 2-HIBA on cognitive dysfunction caused by diabetic encephalopathy (
Fig. 5
E and F). After knocking down ND3, the mitochondrial energy supply function of the brain hippocampal tissue was tested, which showed that 2-HIBA failed to restore NAD
+
/NADH and tissue ATP levels, indicating that the knockout of ND3 blocked the mitochondrial energy supply restored by 2-HIBA and the maintenance of functional homeostasis. NanoLC-Obitrap-MS, SPR, MST, cell thermal shift measurement CETSA, and DART experimental results showed that 2-HIBA can directly enter the mitochondria and bind to ND3, reducing its degradation and enhancing its stability (
Fig. 6
).
Simultaneously, we screened 17 natural medicinal plants for the treatment of diabetes through network pharmacology, and the results showed that Puerariae Lobatae Radix can act on the mitochondrial respiratory electron transport chain and mitochondrial membrane potential, Scutellariae Radix can change mitochondrial membrane permeability and regulate cell apoptosis, Coptis Rhizoma can act on the mitochondrial membrane and respiratory electron transport chain, and A. Membranaceus (Fisch.) Bge. can change mitochondrial apoptosis, Panax ginseng C. A. Mey. can regulate autophagy, and so on. Puerariae Lobatae Radix, Scutellariae Radix, and Coptis Rhizoma can be combined into Gegen Qinlian decoction, and studies have shown that GQD and its main component Pueraria lobata can effectively prevent and treat diabetes by regulating changes in intestinal microbiota and promoting the growth of beneficial bacteria [
63
,
64
]. GQD exerts anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and neuroprotective effects by regulating the intestinal microenvironment [
65
]. A recent review suggests that traditional Chinese medicine acts on the gut microbiota to enhance the production of protective metabolites, such as SCFAs and GABAs [
66
]. Studies have shown that GQD can act on the GABAergic neuron (GABAIN)-pyramidal neuron (GABAIN-PN) pathway in mice to treat neurodegenerative diseases such as dementia and Parkinson's disease [
67
]. GQD can inhibit the apoptosis of hippocampal cells and maintain dendritic density by activating the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway in rats with diabetic cognitive dysfunction, thereby improving learning and memory functions of rats [
68
]. Randomized controlled clinical trials of 60 cases of vascular dementia also showed that GQD improves patients' mini-mental state examination (MMSE) scores and activities of daily living (ADL) scores and effectively prevents further deterioration of the disease [
69
]. In this study, we found that GQD significantly improved cognitive dysfunction (
Fig. 7
A–D) and glucose metabolism disorders in 9-week-old db/db mice after 6 weeks of oral administration (
Fig. 7
E) and did not affect their weight or food intake.
13
C-metabolomics analysis (
Fig. 7
G–I) revealed that oral administration of GQD significantly increased the content of 2-HIBA in the serum of mice. Thus, we confirmed our previous conjecture and proved that GQD acts on MT-ND3 by regulating the differential metabolite 2-HIBA and plays a role in improving cognitive impairment in diabetes by regulating mitochondrial homeostasis.
In conclusion, we herein describe, for the first time, the discovery of 2-HIBA, a fatty acid metabolite derived from intestinal microorganisms, as a valuable therapeutic drug for improving diabetic neuropathy. Its novelty is that it regulates the steady state of blood sugar levels, smoothly penetrates the BBB, enters the affected area of encephalopathy, and directly exerts a neuroprotective effect. This effect may rely on its ability to enter the mitochondria of neuronal cells and directly bind to the mitochondria-encoded protein MT-ND3 to enhance its stability and reduce its degradation rate, thereby maintaining the mitochondrial homeostasis of neuronal cells. This is also the first study to elucidate the biological function of ND3 protein in protecting against neuronal damage. Therefore, selective small molecules targeting MT-ND3 may be a promising proof-of-concept therapeutic strategy for the treatment of diabetic neuropathy. We also explored the agonist of combined medicinal plant (GQD), which can increase the serum 2-HIBA content. These results suggest that it can improve the phenotype of diabetic cognitive dysfunction and increase serum 2-HIBA levels in diseased mice. The next generation of neuroprotective small-molecule metabolites include 2-HIBA, which can be used as a key molecule to study the biological properties of NADH respiratory chain complex enzymes in diabetic neuronal cell damage, and 2-HIBA can be used as potential therapeutic drugs for diabetic cognitive dysfunction.
